Chapter 8: Measuring What Matters and Driving Accountability
As companies grow, keeping tabs on what actually works—and what doesn’t—gets a lot trickier. Without clear metrics, or people you can count on to follow through, teams can end up drifting, or focusing on the wrong things entirely. Measurement gives you clarity. And accountability? That’s what turns promises into real results.
But here’s the thing—measuring what matters isn’t about counting everything that’s easy to track. It means spotting those few numbers that really show you’re making progress toward your biggest goals, and making sure everyone can see them.
So, how do you do that? Let’s look at a few habits that make measurement and accountability stick.
First, pick out your key metrics. What are the handful of indicators that actually move the needle for your business? It could be customer retention, on-time delivery, or even employee engagement. Don’t drown yourself in numbers—just focus on what truly drives your success.
Next, make progress visible. Use simple dashboards or scorecards. For instance, your sales team might keep track of weekly calls, meetings, and closed deals on a shared board everyone can see.
Then, set clear targets. What does success look like for each metric? Maybe it’s a monthly sales goal, or a specific target for reducing customer complaints. The clearer the target, the easier it is to know if you’re winning.
And don’t forget regular check-ins. Use your team meetings to review progress, celebrate wins, and tackle any roadblocks. Hold people accountable for what they’ve committed to, but also offer support and coaching when they need it.
Imagine a nonprofit looking to grow its impact. By tracking things like the number of people served, funds raised, or volunteer hours, the team can spot where they’re moving forward—and where they might need to make a change. Regular reviews keep everyone focused, and fired up to do more.
Remember, measurement and accountability aren’t about micromanaging. They’re about transparency, and making sure everyone shares ownership of the results. When everyone knows where things stand, and feels responsible for the outcome, that’s when your organization really starts moving forward—together.
